entry: Association of artisans or merchants overseeing the practice of a craft or trade in a particular territory. Guilds were most extensive in medieval Europe, though similar groups existed before and after that period and in other parts of the world. Typically, the key privilege of guild members was control of trade in a given city, and guilds might set minimum or maximum prices, hours of trading and numbers of apprentices. Critics argued that these rules reduced free competition, but defenders maintained that guilds protected professional standards. Craft guilds transmitted skills through apprenticeship, journeymanship and mastery, and in major cities such as Florence, [[Paris]] and [[Barcelona]] they became central to economic and civic life. Guilds also maintained welfare funds for sick or elderly members and supported widows and orphans.

Early Renaissance composer and music theorist, variously described as French or Franco-Flemish. Considered the leading European composer of his time, his music was widely performed and reproduced. He was associated with the Burgundian School, particularly his colleague Gilles Binchois, but was never a regular member of the Burgundian chapel. Having joined the papal choir in [[Rome]] in 1428, he wrote his most admired work, the motet *Nuper Rosarum Flores*, which celebrated the consecration of [[Filippo Brunelleschi]]'s dome for the [[Florence Cathedral]]. His later cyclic masses, based on cantus firmus, include *Missa Se la face ay pale*. He has been described as leading the first generation of European musicians who were primarily considered composers by occupation.

French composer and poet, central figure of the *ars nova* style in late medieval music. Regarded as the most significant French composer and poet of the 14th century, he is often seen as the century's leading European composer. Modern musicologists use his death to separate the *ars nova* from the subsequent *ars subtilior* movement. He was crucial in developing the motet and secular song forms, including the lai and the formes fixes: rondeau, virelai and ballade. His *Messe de Nostre Dame* is the earliest known complete setting of the Ordinary of the Mass attributable to a single composer. He was secretary to John I, Count of [[Luxembourg]] and King of [[Bohemia]], from 1323 to 1346, and survived the [[Black Death]]. His poetry was admired and imitated by [[Geoffrey Chaucer]] and Eustache Deschamps.

Mexican filmmaker and actor. His work, strongly connected to [[Fairy tale|fairy tales]], gothicism and horror, often blends the genres. He is known for pioneering dark fantasy in the film industry and has a lifelong fascination with [[Monster|monsters]], which he considers symbols of great power. His films include *Cronos* (1993), *Pan's Labyrinth* (2006) and *The Shape of Water* (2017). His accolades include three [[Academy Awards]], three BAFTA Awards and two Golden Globe Awards. In 2022 he created the [[Netflix]] anthology horror series *Guillermo del Toro's Cabinet of Curiosities*.

Apparatus designed for carrying out executions by beheading. A weighted, angled blade is released from the top of a tall frame and falls onto the neck of the condemned person. The guillotine is best known for its use in France during the [[French Revolution]], where supporters celebrated it as the people's avenger and opponents vilified it as the symbol of the [[Reign of Terror]]. It remained France's standard method of judicial execution until [[Capital punishment|capital punishment]] was abolished in 1981. The last person executed by a government via guillotine was Hamida Djandoubi, a Tunisian murderer, on September 10, 1977, in France.

Moral emotion that arises when a person believes, accurately or not, that they have compromised their own standards of conduct or violated universal moral standards. Guilt is closely related to remorse, regret and [[Shame|shame]]. Understood as a collection of basic emotions, it is composed of self-directed anger, sadness for the victim, [[Anxiety|anxiety]] and fear of damaging relationships. Although unpleasant to feel, guilt can prompt efforts to restore relationships and make amends. [[Sigmund Freud]] attributed guilt to the [[Conscience|conscience]], or superego, and to a fear of loss of love that begins in childhood, and he rejected the role of God. Martin Buber distinguished Freudian guilt, based on internal conflicts, from existential guilt, based on actual harm done to others. Guilt is an important factor in perpetuating [[Obsessive–compulsive disorder]] symptoms.

Coastal country in West Africa, officially the Republic of Guinea. It is sometimes called Guinea-Conakry, after its capital [[Conakry]], to distinguish it from [[Guinea-Bissau]] and Equatorial Guinea. Its area is 245,857 sq km (94,926 sq mi), and it borders the [[Atlantic Ocean]] to the west, [[Mali]] to the northeast and [[Liberia]] to the south. Formerly French Guinea, it achieved independence on October 2, 1958. After decades of authoritarian rule it held its first democratic election in 2010, but a military faction overthrew president Alpha Condé in 2021. It is the world's second-largest producer of [[Bauxite|bauxite]]. Muslims represent 90% of the population, and French is the only language of communication in schools, government and the media.

Country in West Africa, officially the Republic of Guinea-Bissau. It was colonized as Portuguese Guinea in the 19th century, and upon independence the name of its capital, Bissau, was added to the country's name to prevent confusion with [[Guinea]]. Independence was declared in 1973 and recognized in 1974. Parts of the territory were once within the kingdom of Kaabu and the [[Mali Empire]], and some areas had been under Portuguese rule since the 16th century. Portuguese is the official language, though only about 2% of the population speaks it as a first language; Guinea-Bissau Creole is the national language. The nation has followers of [[Islam]], [[Christianity]] and traditional faiths. Since independence, several military coups have interrupted peaceful transfer of power, the latest in 2025, when a military junta headed by transitional president Horta Inta-A Na Man took power. Guinea-Bissau is a member of the [[United Nations]].

Family of birds, Numididae, in the order [[Galliformes]], endemic to Africa. Its members rank among the oldest of the gallinaceous birds and branched off from the core Galliformes after the Cracidae and before the Odontophoridae. These insect- and seed-eating, ground-nesting birds resemble partridges but have featherless heads. Most species have dark grey or blackish plumage with dense white spots. The species for which information is known are normally monogamous. Guinea fowl play a pivotal role in controlling [[Tick|ticks]], [[Fly|flies]], [[Locust|locusts]] and [[Scorpion|scorpions]]. The helmeted guinea fowl has been introduced as a domesticated bird widely elsewhere.

Domesticated [[Rodent|rodent]], *Cavia porcellus*, from South America. Domestic guinea pigs typically weigh 700 to 1,200 g (1.5 to 2.6 lb) and measure 20 to 25 cm (8 to 10 in) in length. They are social animals that are skittish in response to noise or danger. The species was domesticated as early as 5000 BC in the [[Andes]], where it was raised for food and is still consumed, and it is also used in folk medicine and community religious ceremonies. European traders introduced guinea pigs to Europe and North America in the 16th century, and their docile nature has made them popular pets. Animal testing on guinea pigs has been carried out since the 17th century, and the animals were widely used as [[Model organism|model organisms]] in the 19th and 20th centuries. They have since been largely replaced in [[Laboratory|laboratory]] testing by mice and rats, though they are still used in research.

British reference book listing world records of human achievements and the extremes of the natural world. Launched in 1955 as *The Guinness Book of Records*, it was conceived by Sir Hugh Beaver to settle pub debates. Twin brothers Norris and Ross McWhirter co-founded it in London. It is published annually in 100 countries and 40 languages and maintains over 53,000 records. Owned by the Jim Pattison Group since 2008, the franchise has shifted its business away from selling books and toward creating records as publicity for individuals and organizations, a practice that has attracted criticism.

Irish stout originating at St. James's Gate Brewery in [[Dublin]] in the 18th century. Owned by the British multinational Diageo, it is brewed in almost 50 countries and is the highest-selling beer in both Ireland and the United Kingdom. Sales in 2011 amounted to 850,000,000 liters. Its flavor derives from malted [[Barley|barley]] and roasted unmalted barley, and its creamy head comes from mixing the beer with [[Nitrogen|nitrogen]] and carbon dioxide. Arthur Guinness began brewing ales at the site in 1759. The harp motif, modeled on the Trinity College harp, was adopted in 1862 and registered as a trademark in 1876.

Fretted stringed instrument, typically with six or twelve strings, played by strumming or plucking. The guitar is classified as a chordophone, in which a vibrating string is stretched between two fixed points. Its ancestors include the gittern, the vihuela, the four-course [[Renaissance]] guitar and the five-course [[Baroque]] guitar. Steel strings were introduced in the United States near the end of the 19th century, but nylon and steel strings became mainstream only after [[World War II]]. The three main types are the classical guitar, the steel-string acoustic or [[Electric guitar|electric guitar]], and the lap steel guitar. First patented in 1937, the electric guitar made possible effects such as reverb and distortion, and it has played a key role in [[Blues|blues]] and [[Rock music|rock]], notably [[Heavy metal music|heavy metal]] and [[Punk rock|punk rock]]. The guitar is used in a wide variety of genres worldwide.

State on the western coast of India, with the country's longest coastline, about 2,340 km (1,450 mi). Its capital is Gandhinagar and its largest city is [[Ahmedabad]]. The Gujaratis are indigenous to the state, and [[Gujarati language|Gujarati]] is its official language. Covering 196,024 sq km (75,685 sq mi), it is the fifth-largest Indian state by area. It contains 23 sites of the ancient [[Indus Valley Civilisation]], more than any other state, and Lothal is believed to have been one of the world's first seaports. Gujarat is one of four Indian states, with Bihar, Mizoram and Nagaland, to prohibit the sale of alcohol. The Gir National Park is home to the only wild population of the [[Asiatic lion]]. The state's economy is the fourth-largest in India, and it accounts for around one-third of national exports.

Indo-Aryan language native to the Indian state of [[Gujarat]]. It evolved from [[Sanskrit]] and descends from Old Gujarati (c. 1100–1500 CE). It is the official language of Gujarat and one of the 22 scheduled languages of India. As of 2011 it was the sixth most widely spoken language in India, with 55.5 million native speakers, about 4.5% of the population. Gujarati migrants also speak it in [[Mumbai]] and [[Karachi]], and the diaspora is large in North America, especially in New Jersey and New York City. In [[London]] it is the fourth most commonly spoken language. It is also spoken in Southeast Africa, particularly in [[Kenya]], Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia and South Africa, and is written in a script derived from [[Devanagari]].

City in northeastern Punjab province, Pakistan, and headquarters of its eponymous district and division. It is the fourth-largest city in Punjab and the fifth-most populous in Pakistan. Founded in the 18th century, it was the birthplace of Ranjit Singh and served as capital of the Sukerchakia Misl from 1763 to 1799. It was also the capital of the [[Sikh Empire]] from 1799 to 1801, before the capital shifted to [[Lahore]]. Gujranwala is Pakistan's third-largest industrial center after [[Karachi]] and [[Faisalabad]], contributing approximately 5% to 9% to the national GDP. Along with Sialkot and Gujrat, it forms the so-called Golden Triangle of industrial cities with export-oriented economies. Its name means abode of the Gujjars in Punjabi.

Soviet penal labor camp system, operating from the 1930s to the early 1950s. The Gulag was a major instrument of political repression in the [[Soviet Union]], and its camps held both ordinary criminals and political prisoners, many convicted under simplified procedures. The agency that ran the system was established in 1930. After the death of [[Joseph Stalin]], a mass amnesty was granted, and under [[Nikita Khrushchev]] the Gulag was officially abolished on January 25, 1960. Of the 14 million prisoners who passed through the camps and 4 million through the colonies from 1930 to 1953, roughly 1.5 to 1.7 million perished or died soon after release, according to the emerging scholarly consensus. [[Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn]] gave the term international recognition with *The Gulag Archipelago* (1973). Many mining and industrial towns in northern Russia, eastern Russia and Kazakhstan, such as [[Norilsk]], began as blocks of camps built by prisoners.

Warm and swift [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic]] current, part of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation. It originates in the [[Gulf of Mexico]], flows through the Straits of Florida and up the eastern coast of the United States, then veers east near 36°N latitude and moves toward Northwest Europe as the North Atlantic Current. Around 40°N, 30°W it splits in two. The Gulf Stream influences the climate of the coast from [[Florida]] to southeast [[Virginia]] and, to a greater degree, the climate of Northwest Europe. European discovery of the current dates to the 1512 expedition of [[Juan Ponce de León]]. A chart of its path by [[Benjamin Franklin]], based on the observations of a Nantucket whaling captain, was printed in 1769, and satellites from the late 1970s onward have mapped its position in near-real time.

Armed conflict from August 1990 to February 1991 between Iraq and a coalition led by the United States. It followed Iraq's invasion of [[Kuwait]] on August 2, 1990, which drew unanimous resolutions from the [[United Nations Security Council]]. The coalition's operations had two phases: Operation Desert Shield, the military buildup in the Persian Gulf region, and Operation Desert Storm, which began with an air campaign against Iraq on January 17, 1991. A ground offensive from February 24 ended in a ceasefire within 100 hours, and Kuwait was liberated on February 28. Iraqi forces caused over six hundred oil well fires. The war introduced live front-line broadcasts, principally by [[CNN]], and showcased new technologies including [[Satellite|military satellites]], precision-guided munitions and the F-117 Nighthawk stealth aircraft. US bombing of Iraqi chemical weapons facilities is concluded to be the primary cause of Gulf War syndrome, experienced by over 40% of US veterans.

Deepwater gulf of the [[Indian Ocean]] between [[Yemen]] to the north and [[Somalia]] to the south. It connects with the [[Red Sea]] through the Bab-el-Mandeb strait in the northwest and with the [[Arabian Sea]] to the east. Its western end narrows into the Gulf of Tadjoura in [[Djibouti]]. The gulf is part of the [[Suez Canal]] shipping route between the [[Mediterranean Sea]] and the Indian Ocean, with 21,000 ships crossing it annually, and the route is often used to deliver Persian Gulf oil. The Aden Ridge along its middle is widening the gulf by about 15 mm (0.59 in) per year. Isolated fishing towns and villages line its coast, where sardines, tuna, kingfish and mackerel make up the bulk of the catch. The ancient Greeks regarded it as an extension of the Erythraean Sea.

Arm of the [[Pacific Ocean]] defined by the curve of the southern coast of [[Alaska]], between Kabuch Point on the Alaska Peninsula and Cape Spencer. Its shoreline combines forest, mountain and tidewater glaciers, and Lituya Bay is the site of the largest recorded [[Tsunami|tsunami]] in history. Because the North Pacific Current is fed by the warm Kuroshio Current, the gulf remains ice-free throughout the year. It is considered a productive ecosystem, and deep-water [[Coral|corals]] such as *Primnoa pacifica* are found there, typically between 150 and 900 m deep. In 1977 the gulf began an unexpected shift in its climate regime, raising mean sea-surface temperatures and increasing the availability and variety of commercial fish species. The gulf is a great generator of [[Storm|storms]], which dump snow and ice on southern Alaska and often travel south along the coast of [[British Columbia]].

Marginal sea of the [[Pacific Ocean]] that separates the [[Baja California peninsula]] from the [[Mexico|Mexican]] mainland. Also known as the Sea of Cortés, it is bordered by the Mexican states of Baja California, Baja California Sur, Sonora and Sinaloa, and rivers flowing into it include the [[Colorado River]]. The gulf is about 1,126 km (700 mi) long and 48–241 km (30–150 mi) wide. Its maximum depths exceed 3,000 m (9,800 ft), a result of complex geology linked to [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]]. It is thought to be one of the most ecologically diverse seas on Earth, with more than 5,000 species of micro-[[Invertebrate|invertebrates]]. The gulf has 37 major islands, and parts of it are a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site.

Sea off the northern coast of [[Australia]], enclosed on three sides by northern Australia and bounded to the north by the Arafura Sea. It covers a water area of about 300,000 sq km (120,000 sq mi), with a general depth of 55–66 m and a maximum of 69 m. The tidal range is 2–3 m. The Dutch explorer Willem Janszoon was the first European to visit the region, in 1605–06. The gulf was named in 1623 by Jan Carstenszoon in honor of Pieter de Carpentier, governor-general of the Dutch East Indies. It experiences an average of three [[Tropical cyclone|cyclones]] a year, typically between November and April. The Gulf Country to the south supports the world's largest intact savanna woodlands, and a submerged coral reef province in the gulf was recognized only in 2004.

Northeasternmost part of the tropical [[Atlantic Ocean]], extending from Cape Lopez in Gabon north and west to Cape Palmas in [[Liberia]]. Null Island, at the intersection of the Equator and the Prime Meridian, lies within it. The [[Niger River]] is its main river, and the Volta also drains into it. The modern application of the name [[Guinea]] to the coast dates from 1481, when the Portuguese built a fort, São Jorge da Mina (modern-day Elmina), on the Gold Coast. The gulf's coastline includes the Bight of [[Benin]] and the Bight of Bonny. Among the islands, which form part of the Cameroon line of [[Volcano|volcanoes]], is Bioko, under the sovereignty of [[Equatorial Guinea]].

Oceanic basin and marginal sea of the [[Atlantic Ocean]], mostly surrounded by the North American continent. The basin is roughly oval, about 1,500 km (930 mi) wide, and covers about 1.6 million sq km. Almost half of it is shallow [[Continental shelf|continental shelf]] water. It is bounded by the Gulf Coast of the United States, the Mexican states from Tamaulipas to Quintana Roo, and [[Cuba]] on the southeast, and it connects with the [[Caribbean Sea]] through the Yucatán Channel. The gulf is one of the largest offshore [[Petroleum|petroleum]] production regions in the world, making up 14% of total US crude oil production. Its name is associated with the Mexica, the people known as the [[Aztecs]]. The name Gulf of Mexico first appeared on a world map in 1550, and it has been the most common name since the mid-17th century.
